expectedText:
CALIFORNIA FAMILY RIGHTS ACT (CFRA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Acme Corp

COVERED EMPLOYERS
The California Family Rights Act (CFRA) applies to any private employer that directly employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary, and separately to the State of California and any political or civil subdivision of the state and cities, regardless of size.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any person who directly employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(4)(A) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, private-employer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "The state, and any political or civil subdivision of the state and cities."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(4)(B) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, public-employer definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: Five employees is a much lower bar than the federal FMLA, which this corpus's separate FMLA document ties to a 50-employees-within-75-miles worksite test. CFRA's statute doesn't carry forward any worksite-size or geographic-clustering requirement at all — the employer-coverage question under CFRA is simply how many people the employer directly employs, not how many work at the same location. This document doesn't address how 'directly employs' is counted for a business with multiple related entities, franchises, or a staffing-agency arrangement.

WHO IS ELIGIBLE
Jordan Alex Lee is eligible for CFRA leave if Jordan Alex Lee has more than 12 months of service with Acme Corp and has at least 1,250 hours of service with Acme Corp during the previous 12-month period. A separate hours test applies to flight deck and cabin crew employees of air carriers.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "any employee with more than 12 months of service with the employer, and who has at least 1,250 hours of service with the employer during the previous 12-month period or who meets the requirements of subdivision (r), to take up to a total of 12 workweeks in any 12-month period for family care and medical leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(a) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, eligibility and leave grant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: CFRA's eligibility test uses the same two numeric thresholds as the federal FMLA — more than 12 months of service and at least 1,250 hours in the preceding 12-month period — but the statute does not include FMLA's separate worksite-size exclusion (FMLA excludes an employee whose worksite has fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles). CFRA eligibility turns only on the employee's own service with the employer, not on how many coworkers work at the same location. This document doesn't state the specific flight-crew alternative test in subdivision (r), which substitutes a monthly-guarantee percentage and a 504-hour floor for the standard 1,250-hour test.

QUALIFYING REASONS FOR LEAVE
CFRA leave may be taken for the birth of a child or the placement of a child for adoption or foster care; to care for a child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, spouse, domestic partner, or designated person who has a serious health condition; because of the employee's own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the job, other than a disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions; or because of a qualifying exigency related to a spouse's, domestic partner's, child's, or parent's covered active duty in the Armed Forces of the United States.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Leave for reason of the birth of a child of the employee or the placement of a child with an employee in connection with the adoption or foster care of the child by the employee."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(A) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, birth/placement leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "Leave to care for a child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, spouse, domestic partner, or designated person who has a serious health condition."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(B) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, family-care leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "Leave because of an employee’s own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of the position of that employee, except for leave taken for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(C) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, employee's own serious health condition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "Leave because of a qualifying exigency related to the covered active duty or call to covered active duty of an employee’s spouse, domestic partner, child, or parent in the Armed Forces of the United States, as specified in Section 3302.2 of the Unemployment Insurance Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(D) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, qualifying exigency leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: The pregnancy/childbirth exclusion in the third reason is deliberate: California handles pregnancy disability through a separate statute, Government Code Section 12945, not through CFRA — this document doesn't cover that separate law. All four citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2(b)(5) — they are the different parts of one definition, not independent sources confirming each other.

FAMILY MEMBERS COVERED
CFRA defines 'child' to include a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, a child of a domestic partner, or a person to whom the employee stands in loco parentis. It separately defines 'grandparent' as a parent of the employee's parent, 'grandchild' as a child of the employee's child, and 'sibling' as a person related to another by blood, adoption, or affinity through a common legal or biological parent. An employee may also identify one 'designated person' per 12-month period — any individual related by blood or whose association with the employee is the equivalent of a family relationship.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Child” means a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, a child of a domestic partner, or a person to whom the employee stands in loco parentis."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(1) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'child' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "“Designated person” means any individual related by blood or whose association with the employee is the equivalent of a family relationship. The designated person may be identified by the employee at the time the employee requests the leave. An employer may limit an employee to one designated person per 12-month period for family care and medical leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(2) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'designated person' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "“Grandchild” means a child of the employee’s child."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(8) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'grandchild' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "“Grandparent” means a parent of the employee’s parent."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(9) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'grandparent' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "“Sibling” means a person related to another person by blood, adoption, or affinity through a common legal or biological parent."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(14) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'sibling' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: This is materially broader than the FMLA's family-member coverage in this corpus's separate FMLA document, which reaches only a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition. CFRA additionally reaches domestic partners, grandparents, grandchildren, siblings, and one self-identified 'designated person' per 12-month period — categories FMLA's statute does not include at all. All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2(b) — different parts of one set of definitions, not independent sources.

LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Alex Lee requests CFRA leave as described below.

Reason for leave: _______________________________________________
Designated person, if applicable: _______________________________________________
Requested start date: _______________
Expected return date: _______________
Intermittent or reduced schedule (if applicable): _______________________________________________

RETURNING FROM LEAVE
CFRA leave is not deemed granted unless Acme Corp provides Jordan Alex Lee, upon granting the leave request, a guarantee of employment in the same or a comparable position at the end of the leave. During the leave, Jordan Alex Lee retains employee status with Acme Corp, and the leave does not count as a break in service for purposes of longevity, seniority under any collective bargaining agreement, or any employee benefit plan. Jordan Alex Lee returns from leave with no less seniority than Jordan Alex Lee had when the leave began, for purposes of layoff, recall, promotion, job assignment, and seniority-related benefits such as vacation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Family care and medical leave requested pursuant to this subdivision shall not be deemed to have been granted unless the employer provides the employee, upon granting the leave request, a guarantee of employment in the same or a comparable position upon the termination of the leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(a) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, restoration guarantee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "During a family care and medical leave period, the employee shall retain employee status with the employer, and the leave shall not constitute a break in service, for purposes of longevity, seniority under any collective bargaining agreement, or any employee benefit plan. An employee returning from leave shall return with no less seniority than the employee had when the leave commenced, for purposes of layoff, recall, promotion, job assignment, and seniority-related benefits such as vacation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(f) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, employee status and seniority during leave (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "“Employment in the same or a comparable position” means employment in a position that has the same or similar duties and pay that can be performed at the same or similar geographic location as the position held prior to the leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(6) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, 'comparable position' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: 'Comparable position' is itself statutorily defined — one with the same or similar duties and pay that can be performed at the same or similar geographic location as the position held before the leave. It doesn't have to be the identical job, and this document doesn't resolve what counts as 'similar' in a specific case. Unlike this corpus's FMLA document, which quotes a highly-compensated-employee exception letting an employer deny restoration to certain top earners, CFRA's restoration guarantee in subdivision (a) doesn't carry that same statutory exception — this document doesn't independently verify whether any comparable carve-out exists elsewhere in CFRA's implementing regulations, so none is stated here.

NO INTERFERENCE OR RETALIATION
Acme Corp will not interfere with, restrain, or deny Jordan Alex Lee's exercise of, or attempt to exercise, any right provided under CFRA. Acme Corp will not refuse to hire, discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against Jordan Alex Lee because Jordan Alex Lee exercised the right to CFRA leave, or because Jordan Alex Lee gave information or testimony about a CFRA leave request in an inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire, or to discharge, fine, suspend, expel, or discriminate against, any individual because of any of the following: (1) An individual’s exercise of the right to family care and medical leave provided by subdivision (a). (2) An individual’s giving information or testimony as to the individual’s own family care and medical leave, or another person’s family care and medical leave, in any inquiry or proceeding related to rights guaranteed under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(k) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, prohibited discrimination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(q) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, prohibited interference (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2 — different parts of the same section, not independent sources confirming each other.

HOW CFRA RELATES TO FMLA
When Jordan Alex Lee's leave qualifies under both CFRA and the federal FMLA, the two run concurrently: the 12-month period under CFRA runs together with the 12-month period under the FMLA, starting on the date FMLA leave begins, and the combined leave taken under CFRA and FMLA together is capped at 12 workweeks in that 12-month period. Leave taken under the FMLA for a disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions does not count against that combined 12-week cap.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The 12-month period during which 12 workweeks of leave may be taken under this section shall run concurrently with the 12-month period under the FMLA, and shall commence the date leave taken under the FMLA commences."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(o) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, concurrent 12-month period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  "Leave taken by an employee pursuant to this section shall run concurrently with leave taken pursuant to the FMLA, except for any leave taken under the FMLA for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions. The aggregate amount of leave taken under this section or the FMLA, or both, except for leave taken for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions, shall not exceed 12 workweeks in a 12-month period. An employee is entitled to take, in addition to the leave provided for under this section and the FMLA, the leave provided for in Section 12945, if the employee is otherwise qualified for that leave."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(p) (leginfo text), California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, concurrent leave and pregnancy-disability carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12945.2.)
  Known gap: That pregnancy exclusion lines up with the qualifying-reasons clause above: CFRA's own definition of family care and medical leave excludes pregnancy disability, so FMLA leave taken for that reason runs on its own track rather than sharing CFRA's 12 weeks. The statute cross-references a separate law, Government Code Section 12945 (California's pregnancy disability leave law), under which additional leave beyond the 12 weeks described here may be available on top of CFRA and FMLA leave — this document doesn't cover that separate law. All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945.2 — different parts of the same section, not independent sources confirming each other.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge this leave request and the terms above.

Employee: Jordan Alex Lee
Date: _______________
